### 3.3. Enhancing EGT production by identifying and engineering the rate-limiting 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain of NcEGT1
NcEGT1 is a bifunctional enzyme comprising a methyltransferase domain and a 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain [ 47 ] ( Fig. 3 A and B). To identify the rate-limiting step in EGT biosynthesis, we individually overexpressed the methyltransferase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 1-357, named T NC1), 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 358-878, named T NC2) and TrEGT2 based on the E43 strain ( Fig. 3 A). EGT titer analysis revealed that only T NC2 overexpression enhanced EGT production, reaching a titer of 106 mg L −1 , whereas overexpression of T NC1 and TrEGT2 did not improve EGT titer ( Fig. 3 C). These results indicate that the reaction catalyzed by T NC2 constitutes the rate-limiting step in the EGT biosynthetic pathway.
Enhancing the rate-limiting domain of NcEGT1 to improve EGT biosynthesis. (A) EGT biosynthetic pathway and dual-plasmid expression system. (B) Three-dimensional structure of NcEGT1 and mutation sites in T NC2. AlphaFold2 was used to generate the NcEGT1 model and key mutation sites within T NC2 are shown. (C) EGT production after enhancing different enzyme or enzyme domains. Based on E43, T NC1, T NC2 and TrEGT2 (TR2) were enhanced respectively. (D) Effect of T NC2 variants on EGT synthesis. T NC2 variants carrying F478V, F478I, L447D, or G2S/D109A substitutions were expressed in E43. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. In a previous study, Zhang et al. [ 47 ] reported that specific mutations in T NC2 (G2S/D109A, F478I, F478V and L447D) could modulate its enzymatic activity. They noted that residues F478 and L447 are located near the catalytic pocket, suggesting these sites may serve as key functional residues. They further attributed the enhanced enzymatic activity to a potential interaction between the mutated residues serine in position 2 and alanine in position 109 [ 47 ]. ### 3.5. One-strain platform for co-production of EGT, salidroside and gadusol
EGT, salidroside and gadusol are widely used, highly active natural products with important functions including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-photoaging activities, respectively. Moreover, the biosynthetic pathways of these three compounds are relatively independent in metabolism and exhibit minimal cross-interference ( Fig. 5 A), which further establishes the feasibility for constructing a co-production system.

We first achieved independent salidroside and gadusol synthesis in S. cerevisiae , verifying the feasibility of their heterologous expression. Salidroside is synthesized via a regio-specific uridine 5′-diphospho-glucosyltransferase (UGT)-catalyzed tyrosol glycosylation [ 51 ] ( Fig. 5 A). Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for co-production of ergothioneine, salidroside and gadusol

### Abstract
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are high-value cosmetic ingredients valued for their moisturizing, skin-brightening and ultraviolet (UV)-protective properties. Leveraging Saccharomyces cerevisia , a GRAS organism already widely used in cosmetics, we engineered a single strain for their simultaneous co-production. We first identified the 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain reaction as rate-limiting and addressed the poor solubility of ergothioneine biosynthesis protein 1 (EGT1) by screening heterologous homologs and optimizing EGT1 through solubility-enhancing fusions and structure-guided stabilization, increasing EGT titer in shake flask from 34 to 132 mg L −1 . Multicopy integration of the optimized pathway into the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus further boosted EGT production to 690 mg L −1 in a 5-L bioreactor. Subsequently, biosynthetic pathways for salidroside and gadusol were introduced, yielding a tri-product strain that achieved final titers of 1329 mg L −1 EGT, 224 mg L −1 salidroside and 556 mg L −1 gadusol in fed-batch fermentation. This work establishes a multifunctional yeast cell factory capable of simultaneous co-production of multiple premium cosmetic actives, offering a scalable and sustainable platform for next-generation ingredient development.

### 1. Introduction
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are structurally distinct natural bioactive compounds with broad applications in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticas [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] ]. EGT is a sulfur-containing histidine derivative with potent antioxidant activity and has recently garnered attention as a potential longevity-associated micronutrient [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Salidroside, the principal active constituent of Rhodiola species [ 10 ], is widely utilized in functional health products and cosmetic formulations due to its anti-inflammatory and skin-protective properties [ 11 , 12 ]. Gadusol, a naturally occurring mycosporine-like compound originally identified in fish eggs, functions as an endogenous ultraviolet (UV)-absorbing agent and represents a promising candidate for eco-friendly, biodegradable sunscreens and photoprotective cosmetics [ [13] , [14] , [15] ]. The growing market demand for these high-value molecules has spurred interest in developing sustainable, scalable and cost-effective production platforms.
Conventional production methods, including extraction from plants or animals [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] ] and chemical synthesis [ 20 ], are often limited by low yield, high cost and environmental pollution. In contrast, microbial biosynthesis utilizes renewable carbon sources to achieve green, efficient and highly selective targeted production, positioning it as a promising sustainable alternative pathway. To date, individual biosynthetic pathways for EGT, salidroside and gadusol have been successfully reconstructed in various microbial hosts, including Escherichia coli [ [21] , [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] , [26] ] , Corynebacterium glutamicum [ 27 , 28 ] and yeast [ [29] , [30] , [31] , [32] , [33] ]. However, nearly all prior metabolic engineering efforts have focused on single-product synthesis, while integrated strategies for the stable, simultaneous co-production of multiple high-value actives remain largely unexplored.

### 2.3. Media
In this study, E. coli strains were selected and cultivated on Lysogeny Broth (LB) agar plates containing 100 mg L −1 ampicillin (Amp). Subsequent liquid cultures were also grown in LB medium (10 g L −1 tryptone, 5 g L −1 yeast extract and 10 g L −1 NaCl), supplemented with the same concentration of Amp. Yeast competent cells were grown in YPD medium (20 g L −1 tryptone, 10 g L −1 yeast extract and 20 g L −1 glucose). Recombinant yeast strains carrying pESC plasmids were cultured in medium supplemented with 200 mg L −1 geneticin (G418). For solid cultivation, YPD agar medium was prepared by adding 15 g L −1 agar.
Auxotrophic selection was performed using synthetic dropout (SD) medium containing 3.4 g L −1 yeast nitrogen base (YNB), 10 g L −1 ammonium sulfate and 20 g L −1 glucose, supplemented with the required amino acids (histidine, leucine, tryptophan and uracil) at final concentrations of 50 mg L −1 each.

### 2.4. Plasmids construction
Two plasmids (pY26, pESC) were used for constructing gene expression cassettes. All relative primers used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 4 . For this amplification, we used the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae as the template for all native elements, including promoters, genes and terminators. Codon-optimized Ncegt1 , Cpegt1 , Tregt1 , Gfegt1 , Ncegt2 , Cpegt2 , UGT , EEVS and MT-Ox genes were synthesized by GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China). The corresponding DNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3 .

### 2.5. Strain construction
We employed an integrated strain engineering strategy involving plasmid transformation, the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) multicopy integration and Cre/loxP-mediated genome editing for targeted gene overexpression and deletion, following established methodologies. Initially, to achieve heterologous gene expression, the parental S. cerevisiae strain CEN.PK2–1C was transformed with centromeric plasmids. The base EGT-producing strain, designated E1, was constructed by introducing plasmid pESC-NcTr, which carries G418 and Amp resistance and expresses the EGT synthase genes Ncegt1 and Tregt2 . To enhance enzymatic activity, a second centromeric plasmid, pY26-1 (TRP1 marker), was subsequently introduced. For stable and high-level expression, the optimized synthase gene expression cassette was chromosomally integrated into the rDNA locus via Cre/loxP-mediated homologous recombination, yielding a multicopy engineering strain with improved genetic stability and product titer.
Gene integration and marker recycling were performed using the Cre/loxP system. The target gene expression cassette and a loxP-flanked selectable marker were cloned into an integration vector with ∼1000 bp homology arms. The linearized vector was transformed into yeast via the lithium acetate method, and transformants were selected on auxotrophic plates. Positive colonies were randomly picked for shake-flask fermentation.

### 2.7. Fed-batch fermentation in a 5-L bioreactor
A single colony from a YPD agar plate was inoculated into 5 mL YPD medium and incubated overnight at 30 °C and 220 rpm. The seed culture was then inoculated at 2% (v/v) into 50 mL of YPD medium in a 250 mL shake flask and cultivated for 12 h under the same conditions. The resulting culture was inoculated into a 5-L bioreactor to achieve an initial OD 600 of 2.
Fermentation was performed at 30 °C with an initial agitation speed of 300 rpm. The pH was maintained at 5.5 using automatic addition of ammonia water and 30% phosphoric acid. The aeration rate was maintained at 2 vvm, while the agitation speed was adjusted within the range of 300–1200 rpm to keep the dissolved oxygen level at approximately 30% in the fermentation system. When the initial carbon source in the fermentation system is depleted, fed-batch supplementation commences at an initial rate of 12 mL h −1 . The feed solution consisted of 600 g L −1 glucose, 60 g L −1 yeast extract, 1% (v/v) trace element solution and 1.2% (v/v) vitamin solution. After 24 h of cultivation, galactose was added to a final concentration of 2% (w/v) to induce target gene expression. Simultaneously, the amino acid solution was supplemented into the fermentation system at a flow rate of 5 mL h −1 . Using an M-100 biosensor analyzer (Sieman Technology, China) to measure the concentrations of glucose and ethanol in the fermentation supernatant.
Trace element solution: 15 g EDTA, 10.2 g ZnSO 4 ·7H 2 O, 0.5 g MnCl 2 ·4H 2 O, 0.5 g CuSO 4 , 0.86 g CoCl 2 ·6H 2 O, 0.56 g Na 2 MoO 4 ·2H 2 O, 3.84 g CaCl 2 ·2H 2 O and 5.12 g FeSO 4 ·7H 2 O per liter. The solution was sterilized at 121 °C for 15 min and stored at 4 °C.
Vitamin solution: 1 g thiamine hydrochloride (VB 1 ), 1 g niacin (VB 3 ), 1 g calcium pantothenate (VB 5 ), 1 g pyridoxine (VB 6 ), 0.05 g biotin (VB 7 ), 25 g myo-inositol (VB 8 ) and 0.2 g p -aminobenzoic acid (PABA) per liter. The solution was sterilized by filtration and stored at 4 °C.

### 2.10. High-performance liquid chromatography methods
After fermentation, the cultures were centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 2 min to separate the supernatant and pellet. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane for EGT and salidroside analysis. The pellet was resuspended in the original culture volume and subjected to bead-beating with glass beads for cell disruption. The resulting lysate supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and then used for the detection of EGT and gadusol. EGT, salidroside and gadusol were determined using an Agilent 1200 high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system equipped with a C18 column (Thermo Scientific Hypersil GOLD AQ, 250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm).
EGT concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 257 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 1% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.7 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Salidroside concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 275 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 20% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.6 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Gadusol concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 268 nm. Mobile phase A was acetonitrile and Mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid (v/v); the flow rate was 0.3 mL min −1 . The gradient profile was as follows: a linear gradient from 1% A to 90% A (0-10 min), then a linear gradient from 90% A to 100% A (10-20 min), finally return to 1% A for 5 min. The injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 25 min.

### 3. Results and discussion
3.1. Screening and identification of optimal EGT1/EGT2 enzyme combinations for EGT biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae
The biosynthesis of EGT in eukaryotes is catalyzed by two essential enzymes: EGT1 and EGT2 [ 45 ]. EGT1 catalyzes the methylation of l -histidine to give hercynine (HER), followed by its coupling with cysteine to form hercynylcysteine sulfoxide (Cys-HER). EGT2 catalyzes the conversion of Cys-HER to 2-(hydroxysulfanyl)hercynine [ 46 ] ( Fig. 1 A). As S. cerevisiae lacks endogenous EGT biosynthesis capacity, reconstruction of the EGT pathway requires heterologous expression of functional egt1 and egt2 genes.

### 3.2. Improving NcEGT1 soluble expression enhances EGT production
Although strain E1 was capable of producing EGT, its titer remained suboptimal. Previous studies have indicated that the expression of NcEGT1 may serve as a primary bottleneck limiting the synthesis flux [ 47 ]. To identify the key limitations in EGT production, we analyzed the expression levels of NcEGT1 and TrEGT2 by SDS-PAGE. Analysis revealed that NcEGT1 was insoluble and expressed at a low level ( Fig. 2 A). These observations suggest that poor solubility and low expression of NcEGT1 are likely key bottlenecks restricting EGT biosynthetic efficiency.

### 3.3. Enhancing EGT production by identifying and engineering the rate-limiting 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain of NcEGT1
NcEGT1 is a bifunctional enzyme comprising a methyltransferase domain and a 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain [ 47 ] ( Fig. 3 A and B). To identify the rate-limiting step in EGT biosynthesis, we individually overexpressed the methyltransferase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 1-357, named T NC1), 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 358-878, named T NC2) and TrEGT2 based on the E43 strain ( Fig. 3 A). EGT titer analysis revealed that only T NC2 overexpression enhanced EGT production, reaching a titer of 106 mg L −1 , whereas overexpression of T NC1 and TrEGT2 did not improve EGT titer ( Fig. 3 C). These results indicate that the reaction catalyzed by T NC2 constitutes the rate-limiting step in the EGT biosynthetic pathway.
Enhancing the rate-limiting domain of NcEGT1 to improve EGT biosynthesis. (A) EGT biosynthetic pathway and dual-plasmid expression system. (B) Three-dimensional structure of NcEGT1 and mutation sites in T NC2. AlphaFold2 was used to generate the NcEGT1 model and key mutation sites within T NC2 are shown. (C) EGT production after enhancing different enzyme or enzyme domains. Based on E43, T NC1, T NC2 and TrEGT2 (TR2) were enhanced respectively. (D) Effect of T NC2 variants on EGT synthesis. T NC2 variants carrying F478V, F478I, L447D, or G2S/D109A substitutions were expressed in E43. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. In a previous study, Zhang et al. [ 47 ] reported that specific mutations in T NC2 (G2S/D109A, F478I, F478V and L447D) could modulate its enzymatic activity. They noted that residues F478 and L447 are located near the catalytic pocket, suggesting these sites may serve as key functional residues. They further attributed the enhanced enzymatic activity to a potential interaction between the mutated residues serine in position 2 and alanine in position 109 [ 47 ]. ### 3.5. One-strain platform for co-production of EGT, salidroside and gadusol
EGT, salidroside and gadusol are widely used, highly active natural products with important functions including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-photoaging activities, respectively. Moreover, the biosynthetic pathways of these three compounds are relatively independent in metabolism and exhibit minimal cross-interference ( Fig. 5 A), which further establishes the feasibility for constructing a co-production system.

(B) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titer and LC-MS analysis of salidroside. (C) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titer and LC-MS analysis of gadusol. (D) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titers of EGT, salidroside and gadusol. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. We first achieved independent salidroside and gadusol synthesis in S. cerevisiae , verifying the feasibility of their heterologous expression. Salidroside is synthesized via a regio-specific uridine 5′-diphospho-glucosyltransferase (UGT)-catalyzed tyrosol glycosylation [ 51 ] ( Fig. 5 A). Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for co-production of ergothioneine, salidroside and gadusol

### Abstract
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are high-value cosmetic ingredients valued for their moisturizing, skin-brightening and ultraviolet (UV)-protective properties. Leveraging Saccharomyces cerevisia , a GRAS organism already widely used in cosmetics, we engineered a single strain for their simultaneous co-production. We first identified the 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain reaction as rate-limiting and addressed the poor solubility of ergothioneine biosynthesis protein 1 (EGT1) by screening heterologous homologs and optimizing EGT1 through solubility-enhancing fusions and structure-guided stabilization, increasing EGT titer in shake flask from 34 to 132 mg L −1 . Multicopy integration of the optimized pathway into the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus further boosted EGT production to 690 mg L −1 in a 5-L bioreactor. Subsequently, biosynthetic pathways for salidroside and gadusol were introduced, yielding a tri-product strain that achieved final titers of 1329 mg L −1 EGT, 224 mg L −1 salidroside and 556 mg L −1 gadusol in fed-batch fermentation. This work establishes a multifunctional yeast cell factory capable of simultaneous co-production of multiple premium cosmetic actives, offering a scalable and sustainable platform for next-generation ingredient development.

### 1. Introduction
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are structurally distinct natural bioactive compounds with broad applications in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticas [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] ]. EGT is a sulfur-containing histidine derivative with potent antioxidant activity and has recently garnered attention as a potential longevity-associated micronutrient [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Salidroside, the principal active constituent of Rhodiola species [ 10 ], is widely utilized in functional health products and cosmetic formulations due to its anti-inflammatory and skin-protective properties [ 11 , 12 ]. Gadusol, a naturally occurring mycosporine-like compound originally identified in fish eggs, functions as an endogenous ultraviolet (UV)-absorbing agent and represents a promising candidate for eco-friendly, biodegradable sunscreens and photoprotective cosmetics [ [13] , [14] , [15] ]. The growing market demand for these high-value molecules has spurred interest in developing sustainable, scalable and cost-effective production platforms.
Conventional production methods, including extraction from plants or animals [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] ] and chemical synthesis [ 20 ], are often limited by low yield, high cost and environmental pollution. In contrast, microbial biosynthesis utilizes renewable carbon sources to achieve green, efficient and highly selective targeted production, positioning it as a promising sustainable alternative pathway. To date, individual biosynthetic pathways for EGT, salidroside and gadusol have been successfully reconstructed in various microbial hosts, including Escherichia coli [ [21] , [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] , [26] ] , Corynebacterium glutamicum [ 27 , 28 ] and yeast [ [29] , [30] , [31] , [32] , [33] ]. However, nearly all prior metabolic engineering efforts have focused on single-product synthesis, while integrated strategies for the stable, simultaneous co-production of multiple high-value actives remain largely unexplored.

### 2.3. Media
In this study, E. coli strains were selected and cultivated on Lysogeny Broth (LB) agar plates containing 100 mg L −1 ampicillin (Amp). Subsequent liquid cultures were also grown in LB medium (10 g L −1 tryptone, 5 g L −1 yeast extract and 10 g L −1 NaCl), supplemented with the same concentration of Amp. Yeast competent cells were grown in YPD medium (20 g L −1 tryptone, 10 g L −1 yeast extract and 20 g L −1 glucose). Recombinant yeast strains carrying pESC plasmids were cultured in medium supplemented with 200 mg L −1 geneticin (G418). For solid cultivation, YPD agar medium was prepared by adding 15 g L −1 agar.
Auxotrophic selection was performed using synthetic dropout (SD) medium containing 3.4 g L −1 yeast nitrogen base (YNB), 10 g L −1 ammonium sulfate and 20 g L −1 glucose, supplemented with the required amino acids (histidine, leucine, tryptophan and uracil) at final concentrations of 50 mg L −1 each.

### 2.4. Plasmids construction
Two plasmids (pY26, pESC) were used for constructing gene expression cassettes. All relative primers used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 4 . For this amplification, we used the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae as the template for all native elements, including promoters, genes and terminators. Codon-optimized Ncegt1 , Cpegt1 , Tregt1 , Gfegt1 , Ncegt2 , Cpegt2 , UGT , EEVS and MT-Ox genes were synthesized by GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China). The corresponding DNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3 .

### 2.5. Strain construction
We employed an integrated strain engineering strategy involving plasmid transformation, the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) multicopy integration and Cre/loxP-mediated genome editing for targeted gene overexpression and deletion, following established methodologies. Initially, to achieve heterologous gene expression, the parental S. cerevisiae strain CEN.PK2–1C was transformed with centromeric plasmids. The base EGT-producing strain, designated E1, was constructed by introducing plasmid pESC-NcTr, which carries G418 and Amp resistance and expresses the EGT synthase genes Ncegt1 and Tregt2 . To enhance enzymatic activity, a second centromeric plasmid, pY26-1 (TRP1 marker), was subsequently introduced. For stable and high-level expression, the optimized synthase gene expression cassette was chromosomally integrated into the rDNA locus via Cre/loxP-mediated homologous recombination, yielding a multicopy engineering strain with improved genetic stability and product titer.
Gene integration and marker recycling were performed using the Cre/loxP system. The target gene expression cassette and a loxP-flanked selectable marker were cloned into an integration vector with ∼1000 bp homology arms. The linearized vector was transformed into yeast via the lithium acetate method, and transformants were selected on auxotrophic plates. Positive colonies were randomly picked for shake-flask fermentation.

### 2.7. Fed-batch fermentation in a 5-L bioreactor
A single colony from a YPD agar plate was inoculated into 5 mL YPD medium and incubated overnight at 30 °C and 220 rpm. The seed culture was then inoculated at 2% (v/v) into 50 mL of YPD medium in a 250 mL shake flask and cultivated for 12 h under the same conditions. The resulting culture was inoculated into a 5-L bioreactor to achieve an initial OD 600 of 2.
Fermentation was performed at 30 °C with an initial agitation speed of 300 rpm. The pH was maintained at 5.5 using automatic addition of ammonia water and 30% phosphoric acid. The aeration rate was maintained at 2 vvm, while the agitation speed was adjusted within the range of 300–1200 rpm to keep the dissolved oxygen level at approximately 30% in the fermentation system. When the initial carbon source in the fermentation system is depleted, fed-batch supplementation commences at an initial rate of 12 mL h −1 . The feed solution consisted of 600 g L −1 glucose, 60 g L −1 yeast extract, 1% (v/v) trace element solution and 1.2% (v/v) vitamin solution. After 24 h of cultivation, galactose was added to a final concentration of 2% (w/v) to induce target gene expression. Simultaneously, the amino acid solution was supplemented into the fermentation system at a flow rate of 5 mL h −1 . Using an M-100 biosensor analyzer (Sieman Technology, China) to measure the concentrations of glucose and ethanol in the fermentation supernatant.
Trace element solution: 15 g EDTA, 10.2 g ZnSO 4 ·7H 2 O, 0.5 g MnCl 2 ·4H 2 O, 0.5 g CuSO 4 , 0.86 g CoCl 2 ·6H 2 O, 0.56 g Na 2 MoO 4 ·2H 2 O, 3.84 g CaCl 2 ·2H 2 O and 5.12 g FeSO 4 ·7H 2 O per liter. The solution was sterilized at 121 °C for 15 min and stored at 4 °C.
Vitamin solution: 1 g thiamine hydrochloride (VB 1 ), 1 g niacin (VB 3 ), 1 g calcium pantothenate (VB 5 ), 1 g pyridoxine (VB 6 ), 0.05 g biotin (VB 7 ), 25 g myo-inositol (VB 8 ) and 0.2 g p -aminobenzoic acid (PABA) per liter. The solution was sterilized by filtration and stored at 4 °C.

### 2.10. High-performance liquid chromatography methods
After fermentation, the cultures were centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 2 min to separate the supernatant and pellet. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane for EGT and salidroside analysis. The pellet was resuspended in the original culture volume and subjected to bead-beating with glass beads for cell disruption. The resulting lysate supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and then used for the detection of EGT and gadusol. EGT, salidroside and gadusol were determined using an Agilent 1200 high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system equipped with a C18 column (Thermo Scientific Hypersil GOLD AQ, 250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm).
EGT concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 257 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 1% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.7 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Salidroside concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 275 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 20% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.6 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Gadusol concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 268 nm. Mobile phase A was acetonitrile and Mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid (v/v); the flow rate was 0.3 mL min −1 . The gradient profile was as follows: a linear gradient from 1% A to 90% A (0-10 min), then a linear gradient from 90% A to 100% A (10-20 min), finally return to 1% A for 5 min. The injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 25 min.

### 3. Results and discussion
3.1. Screening and identification of optimal EGT1/EGT2 enzyme combinations for EGT biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae
The biosynthesis of EGT in eukaryotes is catalyzed by two essential enzymes: EGT1 and EGT2 [ 45 ]. EGT1 catalyzes the methylation of l -histidine to give hercynine (HER), followed by its coupling with cysteine to form hercynylcysteine sulfoxide (Cys-HER). EGT2 catalyzes the conversion of Cys-HER to 2-(hydroxysulfanyl)hercynine [ 46 ] ( Fig. 1 A). As S. cerevisiae lacks endogenous EGT biosynthesis capacity, reconstruction of the EGT pathway requires heterologous expression of functional egt1 and egt2 genes.

### 3.2. Improving NcEGT1 soluble expression enhances EGT production
Although strain E1 was capable of producing EGT, its titer remained suboptimal. Previous studies have indicated that the expression of NcEGT1 may serve as a primary bottleneck limiting the synthesis flux [ 47 ]. To identify the key limitations in EGT production, we analyzed the expression levels of NcEGT1 and TrEGT2 by SDS-PAGE. Analysis revealed that NcEGT1 was insoluble and expressed at a low level ( Fig. 2 A). These observations suggest that poor solubility and low expression of NcEGT1 are likely key bottlenecks restricting EGT biosynthetic efficiency.

The arrowheads indicate the expected positions of NcEGT1 (≈99 kDa) and TrEGT2 (≈53 kDa). +: soluble crude extract. -: insoluble crude extract. ### 3.3. Enhancing EGT production by identifying and engineering the rate-limiting 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain of NcEGT1
NcEGT1 is a bifunctional enzyme comprising a methyltransferase domain and a 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain [ 47 ] ( Fig. 3 A and B). To identify the rate-limiting step in EGT biosynthesis, we individually overexpressed the methyltransferase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 1-357, named T NC1), 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 358-878, named T NC2) and TrEGT2 based on the E43 strain ( Fig. 3 A). EGT titer analysis revealed that only T NC2 overexpression enhanced EGT production, reaching a titer of 106 mg L −1 , whereas overexpression of T NC1 and TrEGT2 did not improve EGT titer ( Fig. 3 C). These results indicate that the reaction catalyzed by T NC2 constitutes the rate-limiting step in the EGT biosynthetic pathway.
Enhancing the rate-limiting domain of NcEGT1 to improve EGT biosynthesis. (A) EGT biosynthetic pathway and dual-plasmid expression system. (B) Three-dimensional structure of NcEGT1 and mutation sites in T NC2. AlphaFold2 was used to generate the NcEGT1 model and key mutation sites within T NC2 are shown. (C) EGT production after enhancing different enzyme or enzyme domains. Based on E43, T NC1, T NC2 and TrEGT2 (TR2) were enhanced respectively. (D) Effect of T NC2 variants on EGT synthesis. T NC2 variants carrying F478V, F478I, L447D, or G2S/D109A substitutions were expressed in E43. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. In a previous study, Zhang et al. [ 47 ] reported that specific mutations in T NC2 (G2S/D109A, F478I, F478V and L447D) could modulate its enzymatic activity. They noted that residues F478 and L447 are located near the catalytic pocket, suggesting these sites may serve as key functional residues. They further attributed the enhanced enzymatic activity to a potential interaction between the mutated residues serine in position 2 and alanine in position 109 [ 47 ]. ### 3.5. One-strain platform for co-production of EGT, salidroside and gadusol
EGT, salidroside and gadusol are widely used, highly active natural products with important functions including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-photoaging activities, respectively. Moreover, the biosynthetic pathways of these three compounds are relatively independent in metabolism and exhibit minimal cross-interference ( Fig. 5 A), which further establishes the feasibility for constructing a co-production system.

(B) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titer and LC-MS analysis of salidroside. (C) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titer and LC-MS analysis of gadusol. (D) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titers of EGT, salidroside and gadusol. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. We first achieved independent salidroside and gadusol synthesis in S. cerevisiae , verifying the feasibility of their heterologous expression. Salidroside is synthesized via a regio-specific uridine 5′-diphospho-glucosyltransferase (UGT)-catalyzed tyrosol glycosylation [ 51 ] ( Fig. 5 A). ### Abstract
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are high-value cosmetic ingredients valued for their moisturizing, skin-brightening and ultraviolet (UV)-protective properties. Leveraging Saccharomyces cerevisia , a GRAS organism already widely used in cosmetics, we engineered a single strain for their simultaneous co-production. We first identified the 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain reaction as rate-limiting and addressed the poor solubility of ergothioneine biosynthesis protein 1 (EGT1) by screening heterologous homologs and optimizing EGT1 through solubility-enhancing fusions and structure-guided stabilization, increasing EGT titer in shake flask from 34 to 132 mg L −1 . Multicopy integration of the optimized pathway into the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus further boosted EGT production to 690 mg L −1 in a 5-L bioreactor. Subsequently, biosynthetic pathways for salidroside and gadusol were introduced, yielding a tri-product strain that achieved final titers of 1329 mg L −1 EGT, 224 mg L −1 salidroside and 556 mg L −1 gadusol in fed-batch fermentation. This work establishes a multifunctional yeast cell factory capable of simultaneous co-production of multiple premium cosmetic actives, offering a scalable and sustainable platform for next-generation ingredient development.

### 1. Introduction
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are structurally distinct natural bioactive compounds with broad applications in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticas [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] ]. EGT is a sulfur-containing histidine derivative with potent antioxidant activity and has recently garnered attention as a potential longevity-associated micronutrient [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Salidroside, the principal active constituent of Rhodiola species [ 10 ], is widely utilized in functional health products and cosmetic formulations due to its anti-inflammatory and skin-protective properties [ 11 , 12 ]. Gadusol, a naturally occurring mycosporine-like compound originally identified in fish eggs, functions as an endogenous ultraviolet (UV)-absorbing agent and represents a promising candidate for eco-friendly, biodegradable sunscreens and photoprotective cosmetics [ [13] , [14] , [15] ]. The growing market demand for these high-value molecules has spurred interest in developing sustainable, scalable and cost-effective production platforms.
Conventional production methods, including extraction from plants or animals [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] ] and chemical synthesis [ 20 ], are often limited by low yield, high cost and environmental pollution. In contrast, microbial biosynthesis utilizes renewable carbon sources to achieve green, efficient and highly selective targeted production, positioning it as a promising sustainable alternative pathway. To date, individual biosynthetic pathways for EGT, salidroside and gadusol have been successfully reconstructed in various microbial hosts, including Escherichia coli [ [21] , [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] , [26] ] , Corynebacterium glutamicum [ 27 , 28 ] and yeast [ [29] , [30] , [31] , [32] , [33] ]. However, nearly all prior metabolic engineering efforts have focused on single-product synthesis, while integrated strategies for the stable, simultaneous co-production of multiple high-value actives remain largely unexplored.

### 2.3. Media
In this study, E. coli strains were selected and cultivated on Lysogeny Broth (LB) agar plates containing 100 mg L −1 ampicillin (Amp). Subsequent liquid cultures were also grown in LB medium (10 g L −1 tryptone, 5 g L −1 yeast extract and 10 g L −1 NaCl), supplemented with the same concentration of Amp. Yeast competent cells were grown in YPD medium (20 g L −1 tryptone, 10 g L −1 yeast extract and 20 g L −1 glucose). Recombinant yeast strains carrying pESC plasmids were cultured in medium supplemented with 200 mg L −1 geneticin (G418). For solid cultivation, YPD agar medium was prepared by adding 15 g L −1 agar.
Auxotrophic selection was performed using synthetic dropout (SD) medium containing 3.4 g L −1 yeast nitrogen base (YNB), 10 g L −1 ammonium sulfate and 20 g L −1 glucose, supplemented with the required amino acids (histidine, leucine, tryptophan and uracil) at final concentrations of 50 mg L −1 each.

### 2.4. Plasmids construction
Two plasmids (pY26, pESC) were used for constructing gene expression cassettes. All relative primers used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 4 . For this amplification, we used the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae as the template for all native elements, including promoters, genes and terminators. Codon-optimized Ncegt1 , Cpegt1 , Tregt1 , Gfegt1 , Ncegt2 , Cpegt2 , UGT , EEVS and MT-Ox genes were synthesized by GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China). The corresponding DNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3 .

### 2.5. Strain construction
We employed an integrated strain engineering strategy involving plasmid transformation, the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) multicopy integration and Cre/loxP-mediated genome editing for targeted gene overexpression and deletion, following established methodologies. Initially, to achieve heterologous gene expression, the parental S. cerevisiae strain CEN.PK2–1C was transformed with centromeric plasmids. The base EGT-producing strain, designated E1, was constructed by introducing plasmid pESC-NcTr, which carries G418 and Amp resistance and expresses the EGT synthase genes Ncegt1 and Tregt2 . To enhance enzymatic activity, a second centromeric plasmid, pY26-1 (TRP1 marker), was subsequently introduced. For stable and high-level expression, the optimized synthase gene expression cassette was chromosomally integrated into the rDNA locus via Cre/loxP-mediated homologous recombination, yielding a multicopy engineering strain with improved genetic stability and product titer.
Gene integration and marker recycling were performed using the Cre/loxP system. The target gene expression cassette and a loxP-flanked selectable marker were cloned into an integration vector with ∼1000 bp homology arms. The linearized vector was transformed into yeast via the lithium acetate method, and transformants were selected on auxotrophic plates. Positive colonies were randomly picked for shake-flask fermentation.

### 2.7. Fed-batch fermentation in a 5-L bioreactor
A single colony from a YPD agar plate was inoculated into 5 mL YPD medium and incubated overnight at 30 °C and 220 rpm. The seed culture was then inoculated at 2% (v/v) into 50 mL of YPD medium in a 250 mL shake flask and cultivated for 12 h under the same conditions. The resulting culture was inoculated into a 5-L bioreactor to achieve an initial OD 600 of 2.
Fermentation was performed at 30 °C with an initial agitation speed of 300 rpm. The pH was maintained at 5.5 using automatic addition of ammonia water and 30% phosphoric acid. The aeration rate was maintained at 2 vvm, while the agitation speed was adjusted within the range of 300–1200 rpm to keep the dissolved oxygen level at approximately 30% in the fermentation system. When the initial carbon source in the fermentation system is depleted, fed-batch supplementation commences at an initial rate of 12 mL h −1 . The feed solution consisted of 600 g L −1 glucose, 60 g L −1 yeast extract, 1% (v/v) trace element solution and 1.2% (v/v) vitamin solution. After 24 h of cultivation, galactose was added to a final concentration of 2% (w/v) to induce target gene expression. Simultaneously, the amino acid solution was supplemented into the fermentation system at a flow rate of 5 mL h −1 . Using an M-100 biosensor analyzer (Sieman Technology, China) to measure the concentrations of glucose and ethanol in the fermentation supernatant.
Trace element solution: 15 g EDTA, 10.2 g ZnSO 4 ·7H 2 O, 0.5 g MnCl 2 ·4H 2 O, 0.5 g CuSO 4 , 0.86 g CoCl 2 ·6H 2 O, 0.56 g Na 2 MoO 4 ·2H 2 O, 3.84 g CaCl 2 ·2H 2 O and 5.12 g FeSO 4 ·7H 2 O per liter. The solution was sterilized at 121 °C for 15 min and stored at 4 °C.
Vitamin solution: 1 g thiamine hydrochloride (VB 1 ), 1 g niacin (VB 3 ), 1 g calcium pantothenate (VB 5 ), 1 g pyridoxine (VB 6 ), 0.05 g biotin (VB 7 ), 25 g myo-inositol (VB 8 ) and 0.2 g p -aminobenzoic acid (PABA) per liter. The solution was sterilized by filtration and stored at 4 °C.

### 2.10. High-performance liquid chromatography methods
After fermentation, the cultures were centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 2 min to separate the supernatant and pellet. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane for EGT and salidroside analysis. The pellet was resuspended in the original culture volume and subjected to bead-beating with glass beads for cell disruption. The resulting lysate supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and then used for the detection of EGT and gadusol. EGT, salidroside and gadusol were determined using an Agilent 1200 high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system equipped with a C18 column (Thermo Scientific Hypersil GOLD AQ, 250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm).
EGT concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 257 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 1% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.7 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Salidroside concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 275 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 20% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.6 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Gadusol concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 268 nm. Mobile phase A was acetonitrile and Mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid (v/v); the flow rate was 0.3 mL min −1 . The gradient profile was as follows: a linear gradient from 1% A to 90% A (0-10 min), then a linear gradient from 90% A to 100% A (10-20 min), finally return to 1% A for 5 min. The injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 25 min.

### 3. Results and discussion
3.1. Screening and identification of optimal EGT1/EGT2 enzyme combinations for EGT biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae
The biosynthesis of EGT in eukaryotes is catalyzed by two essential enzymes: EGT1 and EGT2 [ 45 ]. EGT1 catalyzes the methylation of l -histidine to give hercynine (HER), followed by its coupling with cysteine to form hercynylcysteine sulfoxide (Cys-HER). EGT2 catalyzes the conversion of Cys-HER to 2-(hydroxysulfanyl)hercynine [ 46 ] ( Fig. 1 A). As S. cerevisiae lacks endogenous EGT biosynthesis capacity, reconstruction of the EGT pathway requires heterologous expression of functional egt1 and egt2 genes.

### 3.2. Improving NcEGT1 soluble expression enhances EGT production
Although strain E1 was capable of producing EGT, its titer remained suboptimal. Previous studies have indicated that the expression of NcEGT1 may serve as a primary bottleneck limiting the synthesis flux [ 47 ]. To identify the key limitations in EGT production, we analyzed the expression levels of NcEGT1 and TrEGT2 by SDS-PAGE. Analysis revealed that NcEGT1 was insoluble and expressed at a low level ( Fig. 2 A). These observations suggest that poor solubility and low expression of NcEGT1 are likely key bottlenecks restricting EGT biosynthetic efficiency.

### 3.3. Enhancing EGT production by identifying and engineering the rate-limiting 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain of NcEGT1
NcEGT1 is a bifunctional enzyme comprising a methyltransferase domain and a 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain [ 47 ] ( Fig. 3 A and B). To identify the rate-limiting step in EGT biosynthesis, we individually overexpressed the methyltransferase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 1-357, named T NC1), 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 358-878, named T NC2) and TrEGT2 based on the E43 strain ( Fig. 3 A). EGT titer analysis revealed that only T NC2 overexpression enhanced EGT production, reaching a titer of 106 mg L −1 , whereas overexpression of T NC1 and TrEGT2 did not improve EGT titer ( Fig. 3 C). These results indicate that the reaction catalyzed by T NC2 constitutes the rate-limiting step in the EGT biosynthetic pathway.
Enhancing the rate-limiting domain of NcEGT1 to improve EGT biosynthesis. (A) EGT biosynthetic pathway and dual-plasmid expression system. (B) Three-dimensional structure of NcEGT1 and mutation sites in T NC2. AlphaFold2 was used to generate the NcEGT1 model and key mutation sites within T NC2 are shown. (C) EGT production after enhancing different enzyme or enzyme domains. Based on E43, T NC1, T NC2 and TrEGT2 (TR2) were enhanced respectively. (D) Effect of T NC2 variants on EGT synthesis. T NC2 variants carrying F478V, F478I, L447D, or G2S/D109A substitutions were expressed in E43. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. In a previous study, Zhang et al. [ 47 ] reported that specific mutations in T NC2 (G2S/D109A, F478I, F478V and L447D) could modulate its enzymatic activity. They noted that residues F478 and L447 are located near the catalytic pocket, suggesting these sites may serve as key functional residues. They further attributed the enhanced enzymatic activity to a potential interaction between the mutated residues serine in position 2 and alanine in position 109 [ 47 ]. ### 3.5. One-strain platform for co-production of EGT, salidroside and gadusol
EGT, salidroside and gadusol are widely used, highly active natural products with important functions including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-photoaging activities, respectively. Moreover, the biosynthetic pathways of these three compounds are relatively independent in metabolism and exhibit minimal cross-interference ( Fig. 5 A), which further establishes the feasibility for constructing a co-production system.

We first achieved independent salidroside and gadusol synthesis in S. cerevisiae , verifying the feasibility of their heterologous expression. Salidroside is synthesized via a regio-specific uridine 5′-diphospho-glucosyltransferase (UGT)-catalyzed tyrosol glycosylation [ 51 ] ( Fig. 5 A). ### Abstract
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are high-value cosmetic ingredients valued for their moisturizing, skin-brightening and ultraviolet (UV)-protective properties. Leveraging Saccharomyces cerevisia , a GRAS organism already widely used in cosmetics, we engineered a single strain for their simultaneous co-production. We first identified the 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain reaction as rate-limiting and addressed the poor solubility of ergothioneine biosynthesis protein 1 (EGT1) by screening heterologous homologs and optimizing EGT1 through solubility-enhancing fusions and structure-guided stabilization, increasing EGT titer in shake flask from 34 to 132 mg L −1 . Multicopy integration of the optimized pathway into the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus further boosted EGT production to 690 mg L −1 in a 5-L bioreactor. Subsequently, biosynthetic pathways for salidroside and gadusol were introduced, yielding a tri-product strain that achieved final titers of 1329 mg L −1 EGT, 224 mg L −1 salidroside and 556 mg L −1 gadusol in fed-batch fermentation. This work establishes a multifunctional yeast cell factory capable of simultaneous co-production of multiple premium cosmetic actives, offering a scalable and sustainable platform for next-generation ingredient development.

### 1. Introduction
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are structurally distinct natural bioactive compounds with broad applications in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticas [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] ]. EGT is a sulfur-containing histidine derivative with potent antioxidant activity and has recently garnered attention as a potential longevity-associated micronutrient [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Salidroside, the principal active constituent of Rhodiola species [ 10 ], is widely utilized in functional health products and cosmetic formulations due to its anti-inflammatory and skin-protective properties [ 11 , 12 ]. Gadusol, a naturally occurring mycosporine-like compound originally identified in fish eggs, functions as an endogenous ultraviolet (UV)-absorbing agent and represents a promising candidate for eco-friendly, biodegradable sunscreens and photoprotective cosmetics [ [13] , [14] , [15] ]. The growing market demand for these high-value molecules has spurred interest in developing sustainable, scalable and cost-effective production platforms.
Conventional production methods, including extraction from plants or animals [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] ] and chemical synthesis [ 20 ], are often limited by low yield, high cost and environmental pollution. In contrast, microbial biosynthesis utilizes renewable carbon sources to achieve green, efficient and highly selective targeted production, positioning it as a promising sustainable alternative pathway. To date, individual biosynthetic pathways for EGT, salidroside and gadusol have been successfully reconstructed in various microbial hosts, including Escherichia coli [ [21] , [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] , [26] ] , Corynebacterium glutamicum [ 27 , 28 ] and yeast [ [29] , [30] , [31] , [32] , [33] ]. However, nearly all prior metabolic engineering efforts have focused on single-product synthesis, while integrated strategies for the stable, simultaneous co-production of multiple high-value actives remain largely unexplored.

### 2.3. Media
In this study, E. coli strains were selected and cultivated on Lysogeny Broth (LB) agar plates containing 100 mg L −1 ampicillin (Amp). Subsequent liquid cultures were also grown in LB medium (10 g L −1 tryptone, 5 g L −1 yeast extract and 10 g L −1 NaCl), supplemented with the same concentration of Amp. Yeast competent cells were grown in YPD medium (20 g L −1 tryptone, 10 g L −1 yeast extract and 20 g L −1 glucose). Recombinant yeast strains carrying pESC plasmids were cultured in medium supplemented with 200 mg L −1 geneticin (G418). For solid cultivation, YPD agar medium was prepared by adding 15 g L −1 agar.
Auxotrophic selection was performed using synthetic dropout (SD) medium containing 3.4 g L −1 yeast nitrogen base (YNB), 10 g L −1 ammonium sulfate and 20 g L −1 glucose, supplemented with the required amino acids (histidine, leucine, tryptophan and uracil) at final concentrations of 50 mg L −1 each.

### 2.4. Plasmids construction
Two plasmids (pY26, pESC) were used for constructing gene expression cassettes. All relative primers used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 4 . For this amplification, we used the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae as the template for all native elements, including promoters, genes and terminators. Codon-optimized Ncegt1 , Cpegt1 , Tregt1 , Gfegt1 , Ncegt2 , Cpegt2 , UGT , EEVS and MT-Ox genes were synthesized by GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China). The corresponding DNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3 .

### 2.5. Strain construction
We employed an integrated strain engineering strategy involving plasmid transformation, the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) multicopy integration and Cre/loxP-mediated genome editing for targeted gene overexpression and deletion, following established methodologies. Initially, to achieve heterologous gene expression, the parental S. cerevisiae strain CEN.PK2–1C was transformed with centromeric plasmids. The base EGT-producing strain, designated E1, was constructed by introducing plasmid pESC-NcTr, which carries G418 and Amp resistance and expresses the EGT synthase genes Ncegt1 and Tregt2 . To enhance enzymatic activity, a second centromeric plasmid, pY26-1 (TRP1 marker), was subsequently introduced. For stable and high-level expression, the optimized synthase gene expression cassette was chromosomally integrated into the rDNA locus via Cre/loxP-mediated homologous recombination, yielding a multicopy engineering strain with improved genetic stability and product titer.
Gene integration and marker recycling were performed using the Cre/loxP system. The target gene expression cassette and a loxP-flanked selectable marker were cloned into an integration vector with ∼1000 bp homology arms. The linearized vector was transformed into yeast via the lithium acetate method, and transformants were selected on auxotrophic plates. Positive colonies were randomly picked for shake-flask fermentation.

### 2.7. Fed-batch fermentation in a 5-L bioreactor
A single colony from a YPD agar plate was inoculated into 5 mL YPD medium and incubated overnight at 30 °C and 220 rpm. The seed culture was then inoculated at 2% (v/v) into 50 mL of YPD medium in a 250 mL shake flask and cultivated for 12 h under the same conditions. The resulting culture was inoculated into a 5-L bioreactor to achieve an initial OD 600 of 2.
Fermentation was performed at 30 °C with an initial agitation speed of 300 rpm. The pH was maintained at 5.5 using automatic addition of ammonia water and 30% phosphoric acid. The aeration rate was maintained at 2 vvm, while the agitation speed was adjusted within the range of 300–1200 rpm to keep the dissolved oxygen level at approximately 30% in the fermentation system. When the initial carbon source in the fermentation system is depleted, fed-batch supplementation commences at an initial rate of 12 mL h −1 . The feed solution consisted of 600 g L −1 glucose, 60 g L −1 yeast extract, 1% (v/v) trace element solution and 1.2% (v/v) vitamin solution. After 24 h of cultivation, galactose was added to a final concentration of 2% (w/v) to induce target gene expression. Simultaneously, the amino acid solution was supplemented into the fermentation system at a flow rate of 5 mL h −1 . Using an M-100 biosensor analyzer (Sieman Technology, China) to measure the concentrations of glucose and ethanol in the fermentation supernatant.
Trace element solution: 15 g EDTA, 10.2 g ZnSO 4 ·7H 2 O, 0.5 g MnCl 2 ·4H 2 O, 0.5 g CuSO 4 , 0.86 g CoCl 2 ·6H 2 O, 0.56 g Na 2 MoO 4 ·2H 2 O, 3.84 g CaCl 2 ·2H 2 O and 5.12 g FeSO 4 ·7H 2 O per liter. The solution was sterilized at 121 °C for 15 min and stored at 4 °C.
Vitamin solution: 1 g thiamine hydrochloride (VB 1 ), 1 g niacin (VB 3 ), 1 g calcium pantothenate (VB 5 ), 1 g pyridoxine (VB 6 ), 0.05 g biotin (VB 7 ), 25 g myo-inositol (VB 8 ) and 0.2 g p -aminobenzoic acid (PABA) per liter. The solution was sterilized by filtration and stored at 4 °C.

### 2.10. High-performance liquid chromatography methods
After fermentation, the cultures were centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 2 min to separate the supernatant and pellet. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane for EGT and salidroside analysis. The pellet was resuspended in the original culture volume and subjected to bead-beating with glass beads for cell disruption. The resulting lysate supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and then used for the detection of EGT and gadusol. EGT, salidroside and gadusol were determined using an Agilent 1200 high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system equipped with a C18 column (Thermo Scientific Hypersil GOLD AQ, 250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm).
EGT concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 257 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 1% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.7 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Salidroside concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 275 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 20% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.6 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Gadusol concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 268 nm. Mobile phase A was acetonitrile and Mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid (v/v); the flow rate was 0.3 mL min −1 . The gradient profile was as follows: a linear gradient from 1% A to 90% A (0-10 min), then a linear gradient from 90% A to 100% A (10-20 min), finally return to 1% A for 5 min. The injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 25 min.

### 3. Results and discussion
3.1. Screening and identification of optimal EGT1/EGT2 enzyme combinations for EGT biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae
The biosynthesis of EGT in eukaryotes is catalyzed by two essential enzymes: EGT1 and EGT2 [ 45 ]. EGT1 catalyzes the methylation of l -histidine to give hercynine (HER), followed by its coupling with cysteine to form hercynylcysteine sulfoxide (Cys-HER). EGT2 catalyzes the conversion of Cys-HER to 2-(hydroxysulfanyl)hercynine [ 46 ] ( Fig. 1 A). As S. cerevisiae lacks endogenous EGT biosynthesis capacity, reconstruction of the EGT pathway requires heterologous expression of functional egt1 and egt2 genes.

### 3.2. Improving NcEGT1 soluble expression enhances EGT production
Although strain E1 was capable of producing EGT, its titer remained suboptimal. Previous studies have indicated that the expression of NcEGT1 may serve as a primary bottleneck limiting the synthesis flux [ 47 ]. To identify the key limitations in EGT production, we analyzed the expression levels of NcEGT1 and TrEGT2 by SDS-PAGE. Analysis revealed that NcEGT1 was insoluble and expressed at a low level ( Fig. 2 A). These observations suggest that poor solubility and low expression of NcEGT1 are likely key bottlenecks restricting EGT biosynthetic efficiency.

### 3.3. Enhancing EGT production by identifying and engineering the rate-limiting 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain of NcEGT1
NcEGT1 is a bifunctional enzyme comprising a methyltransferase domain and a 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain [ 47 ] ( Fig. 3 A and B). To identify the rate-limiting step in EGT biosynthesis, we individually overexpressed the methyltransferase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 1-357, named T NC1), 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 358-878, named T NC2) and TrEGT2 based on the E43 strain ( Fig. 3 A). EGT titer analysis revealed that only T NC2 overexpression enhanced EGT production, reaching a titer of 106 mg L −1 , whereas overexpression of T NC1 and TrEGT2 did not improve EGT titer ( Fig. 3 C). These results indicate that the reaction catalyzed by T NC2 constitutes the rate-limiting step in the EGT biosynthetic pathway.
Enhancing the rate-limiting domain of NcEGT1 to improve EGT biosynthesis. (A) EGT biosynthetic pathway and dual-plasmid expression system. (C) EGT production after enhancing different enzyme or enzyme domains. Based on E43, T NC1, T NC2 and TrEGT2 (TR2) were enhanced respectively. (D) Effect of T NC2 variants on EGT synthesis. T NC2 variants carrying F478V, F478I, L447D, or G2S/D109A substitutions were expressed in E43. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. In a previous study, Zhang et al. [ 47 ] reported that specific mutations in T NC2 (G2S/D109A, F478I, F478V and L447D) could modulate its enzymatic activity. They noted that residues F478 and L447 are located near the catalytic pocket, suggesting these sites may serve as key functional residues. They further attributed the enhanced enzymatic activity to a potential interaction between the mutated residues serine in position 2 and alanine in position 109 [ 47 ]. ### 3.5. One-strain platform for co-production of EGT, salidroside and gadusol
EGT, salidroside and gadusol are widely used, highly active natural products with important functions including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-photoaging activities, respectively. Moreover, the biosynthetic pathways of these three compounds are relatively independent in metabolism and exhibit minimal cross-interference ( Fig. 5 A), which further establishes the feasibility for constructing a co-production system.

(B) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titer and LC-MS analysis of salidroside. (C) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titer and LC-MS analysis of gadusol. (D) Shake-flask fermentation yielded titers of EGT, salidroside and gadusol. (E) Profiles of fed-batch fermentation of E107 concerning cell growth, glucose and ethanol contents and titers of EGT, salidroside and gadusol in a 5-L bioreactor. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. We first achieved independent salidroside and gadusol synthesis in S. cerevisiae , verifying the feasibility of their heterologous expression. Salidroside is synthesized via a regio-specific uridine 5′-diphospho-glucosyltransferase (UGT)-catalyzed tyrosol glycosylation [ 51 ] ( Fig. 5 A). ### Abstract
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are high-value cosmetic ingredients valued for their moisturizing, skin-brightening and ultraviolet (UV)-protective properties. Leveraging Saccharomyces cerevisia , a GRAS organism already widely used in cosmetics, we engineered a single strain for their simultaneous co-production. We first identified the 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain reaction as rate-limiting and addressed the poor solubility of ergothioneine biosynthesis protein 1 (EGT1) by screening heterologous homologs and optimizing EGT1 through solubility-enhancing fusions and structure-guided stabilization, increasing EGT titer in shake flask from 34 to 132 mg L −1 . Multicopy integration of the optimized pathway into the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus further boosted EGT production to 690 mg L −1 in a 5-L bioreactor. Subsequently, biosynthetic pathways for salidroside and gadusol were introduced, yielding a tri-product strain that achieved final titers of 1329 mg L −1 EGT, 224 mg L −1 salidroside and 556 mg L −1 gadusol in fed-batch fermentation. This work establishes a multifunctional yeast cell factory capable of simultaneous co-production of multiple premium cosmetic actives, offering a scalable and sustainable platform for next-generation ingredient development.

### 1. Introduction
Ergothioneine (EGT), salidroside and gadusol are structurally distinct natural bioactive compounds with broad applications in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticas [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] ]. EGT is a sulfur-containing histidine derivative with potent antioxidant activity and has recently garnered attention as a potential longevity-associated micronutrient [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Salidroside, the principal active constituent of Rhodiola species [ 10 ], is widely utilized in functional health products and cosmetic formulations due to its anti-inflammatory and skin-protective properties [ 11 , 12 ]. Gadusol, a naturally occurring mycosporine-like compound originally identified in fish eggs, functions as an endogenous ultraviolet (UV)-absorbing agent and represents a promising candidate for eco-friendly, biodegradable sunscreens and photoprotective cosmetics [ [13] , [14] , [15] ]. The growing market demand for these high-value molecules has spurred interest in developing sustainable, scalable and cost-effective production platforms.
Conventional production methods, including extraction from plants or animals [ [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] ] and chemical synthesis [ 20 ], are often limited by low yield, high cost and environmental pollution. In contrast, microbial biosynthesis utilizes renewable carbon sources to achieve green, efficient and highly selective targeted production, positioning it as a promising sustainable alternative pathway. To date, individual biosynthetic pathways for EGT, salidroside and gadusol have been successfully reconstructed in various microbial hosts, including Escherichia coli [ [21] , [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] , [26] ] , Corynebacterium glutamicum [ 27 , 28 ] and yeast [ [29] , [30] , [31] , [32] , [33] ]. However, nearly all prior metabolic engineering efforts have focused on single-product synthesis, while integrated strategies for the stable, simultaneous co-production of multiple high-value actives remain largely unexplored.
From an i

### 2.3. Media
In this study, E. coli strains were selected and cultivated on Lysogeny Broth (LB) agar plates containing 100 mg L −1 ampicillin (Amp). Subsequent liquid cultures were also grown in LB medium (10 g L −1 tryptone, 5 g L −1 yeast extract and 10 g L −1 NaCl), supplemented with the same concentration of Amp. Yeast competent cells were grown in YPD medium (20 g L −1 tryptone, 10 g L −1 yeast extract and 20 g L −1 glucose). Recombinant yeast strains carrying pESC plasmids were cultured in medium supplemented with 200 mg L −1 geneticin (G418). For solid cultivation, YPD agar medium was prepared by adding 15 g L −1 agar.
Auxotrophic selection was performed using synthetic dropout (SD) medium containing 3.4 g L −1 yeast nitrogen base (YNB), 10 g L −1 ammonium sulfate and 20 g L −1 glucose, supplemented with the required amino acids (histidine, leucine, tryptophan and uracil) at final concentrations of 50 mg L −1 each.

### 2.4. Plasmids construction
Two plasmids (pY26, pESC) were used for constructing gene expression cassettes. All relative primers used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 4 . For this amplification, we used the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae as the template for all native elements, including promoters, genes and terminators. Codon-optimized Ncegt1 , Cpegt1 , Tregt1 , Gfegt1 , Ncegt2 , Cpegt2 , UGT , EEVS and MT-Ox genes were synthesized by GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China). The corresponding DNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3 .

### 2.5. Strain construction
We employed an integrated strain engineering strategy involving plasmid transformation, the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) multicopy integration and Cre/loxP-mediated genome editing for targeted gene overexpression and deletion, following established methodologies. Initially, to achieve heterologous gene expression, the parental S. cerevisiae strain CEN.PK2–1C was transformed with centromeric plasmids. The base EGT-producing strain, designated E1, was constructed by introducing plasmid pESC-NcTr, which carries G418 and Amp resistance and expresses the EGT synthase genes Ncegt1 and Tregt2 . To enhance enzymatic activity, a second centromeric plasmid, pY26-1 (TRP1 marker), was subsequently introduced. For stable and high-level expression, the optimized synthase gene expression cassette was chromosomally integrated into the rDNA locus via Cre/loxP-mediated homologous recombination, yielding a multicopy engineering strain with improved genetic stability and product titer.
Gene integration and marker recycling were performed using the Cre/loxP system. The target gene expression cassette and a loxP-flanked selectable marker were cloned into an integration vector with ∼1000 bp homology arms. The linearized vector was transformed into yeast via the lithium acetate method, and transformants were selected on auxotrophic plates. Positive colonies were randomly picked for shake-flask fermentation.

### 2.7. Fed-batch fermentation in a 5-L bioreactor
A single colony from a YPD agar plate was inoculated into 5 mL YPD medium and incubated overnight at 30 °C and 220 rpm. The seed culture was then inoculated at 2% (v/v) into 50 mL of YPD medium in a 250 mL shake flask and cultivated for 12 h under the same conditions. The resulting culture was inoculated into a 5-L bioreactor to achieve an initial OD 600 of 2.
Fermentation was performed at 30 °C with an initial agitation speed of 300 rpm. The pH was maintained at 5.5 using automatic addition of ammonia water and 30% phosphoric acid. The aeration rate was maintained at 2 vvm, while the agitation speed was adjusted within the range of 300–1200 rpm to keep the dissolved oxygen level at approximately 30% in the fermentation system. When the initial carbon source in the fermentation system is depleted, fed-batch supplementation commences at an initial rate of 12 mL h −1 . The feed solution consisted of 600 g L −1 glucose, 60 g L −1 yeast extract, 1% (v/v) trace element solution and 1.2% (v/v) vitamin solution. After 24 h of cultivation, galactose was added to a final concentration of 2% (w/v) to induce target gene expression. Simultaneously, the amino acid solution was supplemented into the fermentation system at a flow rate of 5 mL h −1 . Using an M-100 biosensor analyzer (Sieman Technology, China) to measure the concentrations of glucose and ethanol in the fermentation supernatant.
Trace element solution: 15 g EDTA, 10.2 g ZnSO 4 ·7H 2 O, 0.5 g MnCl 2 ·4H 2 O, 0.5 g CuSO 4 , 0.86 g CoCl 2 ·6H 2 O, 0.56 g Na 2 MoO 4 ·2H 2 O, 3.84 g CaCl 2 ·2H 2 O and 5.12 g FeSO 4 ·7H 2 O per liter. The solution was sterilized at 121 °C for 15 min and stored at 4 °C.
Vitamin solution: 1 g thiamine hydrochloride (VB 1 ), 1 g niacin (VB 3 ), 1 g calcium pantothenate (VB 5 ), 1 g pyridoxine (VB 6 ), 0.05 g biotin (VB 7 ), 25 g myo-inositol (VB 8 ) and 0.2 g p -aminobenzoic acid (PABA) per liter. The solution was sterilized by filtration and stored at 4 °C.

### 2.10. High-performance liquid chromatography methods
After fermentation, the cultures were centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 2 min to separate the supernatant and pellet. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane for EGT and salidroside analysis. The pellet was resuspended in the original culture volume and subjected to bead-beating with glass beads for cell disruption. The resulting lysate supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and then used for the detection of EGT and gadusol. EGT, salidroside and gadusol were determined using an Agilent 1200 high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system equipped with a C18 column (Thermo Scientific Hypersil GOLD AQ, 250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm).
EGT concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 257 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 1% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.7 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Salidroside concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 275 nm. The mobile phase consisted of 20% methanol (v/v) in water (aqueous phase) and pure methanol (organic phase). The flow rate was 0.6 mL min −1 , the injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 20 min.
Gadusol concentrations were determined using a UV detector set at 268 nm. Mobile phase A was acetonitrile and Mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid (v/v); the flow rate was 0.3 mL min −1 . The gradient profile was as follows: a linear gradient from 1% A to 90% A (0-10 min), then a linear gradient from 90% A to 100% A (10-20 min), finally return to 1% A for 5 min. The injection volume was 5 μL and the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C. Each run lasted 25 min.

### 3. Results and discussion
3.1. Screening and identification of optimal EGT1/EGT2 enzyme combinations for EGT biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae
The biosynthesis of EGT in eukaryotes is catalyzed by two essential enzymes: EGT1 and EGT2 [ 45 ]. EGT1 catalyzes the methylation of l -histidine to give hercynine (HER), followed by its coupling with cysteine to form hercynylcysteine sulfoxide (Cys-HER). EGT2 catalyzes the conversion of Cys-HER to 2-(hydroxysulfanyl)hercynine [ 46 ] ( Fig. 1 A). As S. cerevisiae lacks endogenous EGT biosynthesis capacity, reconstruction of the EGT pathway requires heterologous expression of functional egt1 and egt2 genes.

### 3.2. Improving NcEGT1 soluble expression enhances EGT production
Although strain E1 was capable of producing EGT, its titer remained suboptimal. Previous studies have indicated that the expression of NcEGT1 may serve as a primary bottleneck limiting the synthesis flux [ 47 ]. To identify the key limitations in EGT production, we analyzed the expression levels of NcEGT1 and TrEGT2 by SDS-PAGE. Analysis revealed that NcEGT1 was insoluble and expressed at a low level ( Fig. 2 A). These observations suggest that poor solubility and low expression of NcEGT1 are likely key bottlenecks restricting EGT biosynthetic efficiency.

### 3.3. Enhancing EGT production by identifying and engineering the rate-limiting 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain of NcEGT1
NcEGT1 is a bifunctional enzyme comprising a methyltransferase domain and a 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain [ 47 ] ( Fig. 3 A and B). To identify the rate-limiting step in EGT biosynthesis, we individually overexpressed the methyltransferase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 1-357, named T NC1), 5-histidylcysteine sulfoxide synthase domain fragment of NcEGT1 (residues 358-878, named T NC2) and TrEGT2 based on the E43 strain ( Fig. 3 A). EGT titer analysis revealed that only T NC2 overexpression enhanced EGT production, reaching a titer of 106 mg L −1 , whereas overexpression of T NC1 and TrEGT2 did not improve EGT titer ( Fig. 3 C). These results indicate that the reaction catalyzed by T NC2 constitutes the rate-limiting step in the EGT biosynthetic pathway.

(C) EGT production after enhancing different enzyme or enzyme domains. Based on E43, T NC1, T NC2 and TrEGT2 (TR2) were enhanced respectively. (D) Effect of T NC2 variants on EGT synthesis. T NC2 variants carrying F478V, F478I, L447D, or G2S/D109A substitutions were expressed in E43. All data presented as mean ± S.D. from three (n = 3) biological independent replicates. In a previous study, Zhang et al. [ 47 ] reported that specific mutations in T NC2 (G2S/D109A, F478I, F478V and L447D) could modulate its enzymatic activity. They noted that residues F478 and L447 are located near the catalytic pocket, suggesting these sites may serve as key functional residues. They further attributed the enhanced enzymatic activity to a potential interaction between the mutated residues serine in position 2 and alanine in position 109 [ 47 ]. ### 3.5. One-strain platform for co-production of EGT, salidroside and gadusol
EGT, salidroside and gadusol are widely used, highly active natural products with important functions including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-photoaging activities, respectively. Moreover, the biosynthetic pathways of these three compounds are relatively independent in metabolism and exhibit minimal cross-interference ( Fig. 5 A), which further establishes the feasibility for constructing a co-production system.
